artist: Guy Blackman & Ben O’Connor / Chapter Music
title: Breaking And Entering: Guy Blackman and Ben O’Connor On Chapter Music’s Iconic Catalog and Their Final Releases
summary: After 30 years and over 200 releases, beloved independent label Chapter Music are releasing their final new records. Founder, Guy Blackman and co-founder, Ben O’Connor, take a look back on the label’s evolution from their DIY beginnings at RTRFM in Perth to their latest release with Teether & Kuya Neil. Listen in to hear Guy and Ben open up about the different scenes the label’s adapted to and the legacy that Chapter Music will leave.
transcript:
Guy Blackman and Ben O'Connor of Chapter Music joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios as the label released its final new records after more than 30 years, ahead of its End of an Era party at RISING. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 22 May 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Well, it’s a bittersweet moment for us as we celebrate the legacy of the incredible Chapter Music. Before we get into some questions, we really do have to gush, because this is an emotional moment for us. For those coming to Chapter Music more recently: you have both spent 33 years essentially shaping the sounds of this country’s independent music scene. What began, Guy, as a personal project to document your immediate community evolved into a powerhouse label that’s been responsible for launching countless careers. We heard Laura Jean in there; of course, there’s Twerps, the Goon Sax, Teether and Kuya Neil, and too many more. We worked out that there’s pretty much a Chapter Music band for every letter of the alphabet, which is very appropriate given the literary ties of the label’s name. You’ve consciously championed a really diverse range of artists, and you’ve built the world you want to see: inclusive, artist-driven and community-focused. It’s such a thrill to have you with us. How are you feeling on the eve of this farewell show, and the beginning of a new chapter?

Guy: Yeah, it’s strange, obviously. We’re going through lots of mixed emotions, the happy and the sad. It’s very bittersweet. But we’re feeling very zen, I think, overall.

Ben: I’m just feeling a little bit touched, kind of grateful or whatever, feeling very spiritual about just how much amazing music we’ve gotten to be involved in over the years, and how lucky we are to have worked with so many incredible artists.

Simon: That’s beautiful. You mentioned that people have been reaching out, artists and fans. Are you comfortable sharing some of the things you’re hearing from people?

Ben: It has been really lovely having people we don’t know message us, but it’s also really meaningful having a bunch of bands and artists we’ve worked with getting in touch and saying nice things.

Guy: Yeah, we sent out a big email at the start of the year, or at some stage, warning people, making an official announcement to the artists that this was happening. And, yeah, we did get so many nice replies. There are artists we haven’t put a record out for in, like, decades, artists we worked with in the ’90s or the 2000s, that we still really love, and whose music is still on the Chapter catalogue. So it’s just a lot of people across a long time, and it was quite overwhelming getting a bit of an influx all at once, once we sent that message, from everyone being like, ‘Oh, sorry to hear this, and thanks, and loved working with you,’ et cetera, et cetera.

Ben: I’m not much of a nostalgic person generally, but it has been pretty overwhelming over the last month or so.

Lauren: The influence and legacy is enormous, and really reaches into every corner of the music community here, which is so special. For regular Triple R listeners, the story of Chapter Music will be a familiar one, but for those who’ve discovered your releases more recently, let’s go back to the early days and where it all started. You’ve said that running a label is about creating the world you want to see, a world where art and individual expression are paramount, and where community is incredibly important. I think that might have been you, Ben. Could you expand on how that personal philosophy shaped Chapter Music’s roster and its identity over the decades?

Ben: Well, I think initially it maybe wasn’t as intentional or conscious. When Guy started the label, it was very much about documenting his immediate community.

And I think, I don’t know, it’s difficult to sum up the philosophy of it, or how these things have come about. Things like, we’ve released very few acts that are all straight white men, kind of thing. That was never really an intentional thing originally. It was always just the kind of stuff we were drawn to, before we started realising, ‘Oh, this is kind of what we do.’ And it’s obviously not a hard and fast rule. We have put out bands of all straight white men, because the music they’ve made is amazing, but it hasn’t necessarily always been something we’re drawn to.

But I think just as people, community has always been important to us. And we’re both also people who are really attracted to very personal expressions that people make. We’re really attracted to art that could only have been made by that particular person.

Lauren: Anything you want to add, Guy?

Guy: I think you said everything that I was thinking. I guess we’ve been a couple since 1995, and at that time there was less visibility for queer artists than there is now. In some ways it goes up and down; the ’90s were a pretty queer decade too. But we felt like we were trying to foreground some voices that weren’t as often heard at the time, or over the years: female artists, queer artists (there’s always more work to be done), people of colour, trying not to just contribute to the monolith of the standard Australian rock music or whatever.

Simon: You just talked about the ’90s. Chapter Music is an institution that spans 33 years, and it’s an unfolding story, because of course it will continue in new forms. Throughout that time, you’ve provided a platform for artists across the spectrum, and you’ve seen a lot of changes in the music industry: what the ’90s looked like compared to now is profoundly different. Do you identify chapters within the Chapter Music history, eras you can identify clearly? What are some of the chapters?

Guy: There’s probably micro chapters.

Ben: There’s a hundred of them.

Guy: The first few years were the cassette years in Perth, when I was a teenager, basically putting out cassette compilations of Perth bands. And then I moved to Melbourne in 1995. I’d met Ben in, like, 1994, the very end of ’94 or the very start of ’95, on a visit over from Perth.

Simon: Beautifully documented in Adult Baby as well, your debut album.

Guy: So, yeah, then in that mid-’90s era, I got a job at the vinyl record pressing factory too, so that was the seven-inch vinyl era of the label. And that kind of lasted. CDs started coming in, kind of grudgingly. We were late adopters of CDs, because I was just a big vinyl fanatic, and both of us had a preference.

Then we moved to Japan in the early 2000s. At that point we were like, ‘The label’s finishing.’ It had been 10 years, and we weren’t sure we were going to keep the label going once we got back. But we spent a year and a half in Japan, seeing all this amazing Japanese music, and that just inspired us, as soon as we got back to Australia in 2004, to start putting out some of that Japanese music and documenting it. And then it’s just kind of snowballed again from there.

Simon: Since then, are there other eras?

Guy: I guess we were talking a bit about how, right after that, the late 2000s into the early 2010s was the blog era. Suddenly all our bands were getting written about by these up-and-coming music websites from around the world. We weren’t really too aware of their significance at first, but when Pitchfork and The Fader and Stereogum and all these places started discovering our releases, that kind of —

Ben: I think when that started happening, we made a conscious decision to really kind of chase it.

Guy: At that time, I knew it was hard to get attention in Australia for the kind of Australian music we were interested in.

Simon: Apart from community radio.

Guy: Yeah, apart from Triple R and other community stations. So, yeah, we were trying to sidestep the accepted avenues by going overseas and getting these tastemakers excited about Chapter, and then that would in turn get other people back here excited about us.

Ben: That’s often the way it works with the wider Australian music industry. Obviously there’s the underground, and then there’s community radio, which has always supported interesting shit, interesting stuff that’s going on here. Pardon my French. But I think there’s always been a thing where the wider Australian music industry doesn’t start paying attention to interesting Australian music until it starts getting attention overseas. So we were like, ‘Let’s just go straight overseas.’

Guy: So, yeah, bands like Crayon Fields and Fabulous Diamonds, and then Twerps and Dick Diver, all started to benefit from that, and I guess that was an era. I’m not sure when that came to an end, sometime in the mid-2010s or something.

Simon: And since then, what have the last 10 years been?

Ben: Just Chapter’s adult era.

Lauren: There have been so many incredible Chapter releases, and a real victory lap of final new releases: Teether and Kuya Neil’s new album, a great new EP from Npcede, and of course, Guy, your own second album, which is very exciting. Can you tell us a bit more about these, and what they say about the depth and breadth of the label?

Guy: I guess the Teether and Kuya Neil record is a really satisfying culmination of the relationship we’ve had with them for the last four years or so. I think Ben heard them on Triple R.

Ben: I did. I heard them on Good Static for the first time, a song from their first EP. And from the very first time I heard it, I was just like, ‘We have to work with these.’

Guy: And I was like, ‘They’re not going to want to work with us.’ We’re old white dags who put out lots of non-hip-hop music. But then we set up a meeting with them, and immediately we found we had so much in common that we didn’t realise we were going to, such a similar approach to the way we do things, that it just seemed to gel and became this really beautiful relationship. So working towards their debut album, after the two mixtapes we’ve done, has been a real, real big, long, complicated and rewarding process.

Lauren: They’ve been thrilled with the relationship as well. We were very fortunate to speak with Kuya Neil a couple of weeks ago about the brilliant new album.

Ben: Yeah, it’s like the best hip-hop record ever made in this country, I reckon.

Guy: I feel like maybe we’re not — are we the most qualified people to make that statement? I don’t know.

Simon: That’s a pretty definitive statement to make. I think it’s really an extraordinary record, which breaks so many boundaries and takes in so many different international but very hyper-local styles as well. One thing we loved discovering during that interview was about you, Ben: Kuya Neil was saying how good you are at sequencing records. When did you know you had the superpower?

Ben: I can’t remember what the first record we put out that I sequenced was, but I think it was something I always used to do: when people were sending us demos or tracks before they’d completed the record or whatever, I would always make playlists of how I liked listening to them. And quite often bands would be like, ‘We’re not exactly sure what sequence we want to go with for this record.’ I’ve probably done it for a lot. Lots of acts will have, ‘This is definitely how we want it, and we know,’ and I don’t ever want to interfere with that if someone has their own vision. But if someone asks for help, or is prevaricating and not making decisions, then —

Simon: Happy to bring your impeccable ears to the project and make some decisions.

Guy: And with Npcede, I guess that was just something we were really, really excited about: the idea of going out with a bang, and doing something really unexpected as one of our final releases. We were already quite well advanced into the mechanics, in our heads, of how this was going to happen when we saw their very first show, like a year ago, two years ago.

We already knew this was on the cards, but we were like, ‘Why don’t we sign this artist and release their debut record as one of our very final releases?’ I think we saw them and were just completely gobsmacked and blown away within a minute of their set starting, and then progressively, as the set went on, we saw just how good and how interesting they were for a band playing their first ever show. We were talking about it while they were playing.

Ben: It’s quite liberating, really: let’s put out a record, and then they can go off and do whatever they want. We don’t have the attachments. We’re basically proffering them up on a silver platter to the rest of the music world, to be like, ‘Look at this incredible band. You should snatch them away from us and sign them and make them mega famous.’

Guy: I just think that they’re a band that could be enormous like that.

Ben: I think they’re one of the most exciting bands in the world. They’re just phenomenal, and seeing the progression they’ve had over the time we’ve known them has been astounding.

Guy: And then I guess my solo album had to come last, really, because I just wouldn’t have been able to focus on it with all the other stuff going on. I made a solo album like 15 years ago. I came back from Japan in 2004 all revved up, like, ‘This is my time to be a solo guy and make my statement as an artist.’ And it took me like three or four years to put that record out.

And then after that I was like, ‘Oh, that was exhausting and confronting.’ Putting yourself out into the world as a songwriter and a performer is scary, especially in the late 2000s, as a gay songwriter writing these really personal gay songs. I was like, ‘People aren’t responding. People are still uncomfortable. I’m making them uncomfortable, and that’s making me uncomfortable.’

But a lot’s changed since then, and the end of the record label, or this transition, is partly also just to remind myself that I’m an artist and a musician too. So I wanted the record to have a little bit of space at the end of the label to have its own moment. And it’s a really nice feeling to have a record out again, finally. For a long time, I gave up thinking it would ever happen.

I guess when I started, when we started Chapter, it was very natural for me to be playing music and putting out other people’s music. It was very low-stakes cassettes and the occasional seven-inch, and everyone was just all friends, and we were all kids. But as things went on, it just became more complicated. So it’s very nice.

Ben: The label is still going to keep going. Reissues used to be maybe 25 per cent of what we were doing, so we’re going to keep going at a quarter of the pace. From now on, we’re still going to put out the occasional reissue of old music from the past. But I think it’s just time for us to have this change.

Simon: Yeah, absolutely. And as you say, continuing to platform incredible music strengthens the connections with the past, but also lets us look ahead through that lens. There was a great article Lauren and I were reading, by Brodie Lancaster in Fairfax Press: recommended reading for anyone who hasn’t had a chance to check it out. There’s one quote from it, a powerful statement you made, Ben, about what you’re trying to do now.

Ben: I think when I said that, we were talking about both of the new releases we’re doing, Teether and Kuya Neil, and Npcede. I think I was also specifically talking about the RISING show we’re doing, because with the RISING show, we’ve tried to cover as many bases as possible: what Chapter has been in the past, what it is now, what it could be in the future.

But also, we have a couple of guests who are non-Chapter-related playing the party, like Sidney Phillips, this incredible rapper from Brisbane, who I think is moving to Melbourne, if she hasn’t already moved, who I am just completely obsessed with, and who I think is one of the most exciting things in the country right now. And we also have a person I think is the best songwriter in the world right now, Ryan Davis from Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band.

Guy: Excuse me, I’m right here.

Ben: One of the top, one of the top three songwriters in the world, alongside Guy Blackman and Lana Del Rey.

Guy: I’m happy with that.

Ben: And both of those people, I guess, we chose because we love the music they make, but also, Sidney has her own collective, stealthyn00b, a bunch of rappers and producers, most of them from Brisbane, I think. And Ryan has his own label, Sophomore Lounge. We kind of wanted to connect to other — we might be ending, but there are so many interesting things happening here and around the world, if you just look for them a little bit.

Lauren: The End of an Era show is happening at Max Watt’s as part of RISING’s Day Tripper. It’s a huge line-up. Do you want to talk us through the rest of it?

Guy: Yeah. We’ve got Npcede, who are our newest signing, so it’s stretching from stuff connected to the ’90s, like myself (I’m performing) and Little Ugly Girls, who we’ve been going to see since, like, 1995 or something like that, who are also performing, all the way up to Npcede, who are the youngest and newest artists on the label.

Then we’ve got Tenniscoats coming from Japan, who are one of the best live bands in the whole world, really, and have had this legendary 25-year career of amazing, wistful psychedelic folk and pop.

And then we’ve got Gregor playing this career overview set, which he’s never really done before. He’s always focused on whatever record he’s working on at the time, but this is looking at the four albums he’s done through Chapter, and —

Ben: It’s the greatest hits set.

Guy: Playing it with a full band.

Ben: It’s going to be really, really special. People are just going to cry hearing the song about holding hands live again.

Guy: And then Sidney Phillips, as Ben has said, and Ryan Davis, and Andras and Oscar finishing off the night. That was one of the first records we did where we were like, ‘We can put out a club electronic record. Chapter can be anything.’ It was a real example of us challenging ourselves to widen the parameters of the record label, and another really, really, really satisfying new relationship, and a really well-received classic album: that Café Romantica record we did in 2013 or something like that.

Ben: It was such a fun record to work on with Andras and Oscar. And they never play. But I know that they’re working on new music and have some incredible stuff recorded, so I’m really hoping we see a new album from them sometime in the next year or so.

Lauren: Wow, that’s a tantalising rumour. I love it.

Ben: I don’t know if I’m going to reveal that.

Lauren: That’s amazing. Let’s pressure them out.
aliases: Guy Blackman and Ben O’Connor On Chapter Music’s Iconic Catalog and Their Final Releases
